notes.6: In this question, one distractor proved particularly popular, with a quarter of responses being B. These candidates believed the cuboid to be the most stable, rather than looking for the lowest centre of mass. �PAGE�5
notes.9: The calculation of density caused very few problems in this question, in which 92% of responses were correct.
notes.11: A sizeable number confused force and moment in this question, thus choosing distractor C.
notes.12: This concerned transfer of energy from gravitational potential into other forms, and was very well answered.
notes.13: In this question a common misunderstanding led to a belief that nuclear energy in a power station is first converted into chemical energy, rather than into thermal energy.
notes.20: As many candidates opted for B or C rather than the correct response, showing confusion over the concept of thermal capacity.
notes.21: Almost a third of candidates failed to gain a mark in this question, incorrectly dividing time by the number of waves.
notes.23: This question on the cause of reflection was well answered.
notes.24: The majority of candidates could recognise a reflected image.
notes.25: Only half of the candidates showed a good understanding of the term ‘wavefront’.
notes.27: Most candidates could identify a beam of electrons as being an electric current, either from knowledge of electrons as the charge carriers in metals, or by deducing that electrons were the only charged particles given.
notes.29: This question required an understanding of the potential divider. Approximately half the candidates chose the correct response, with the rest generally opting for C (the opposite of the correct answer).
notes.33: The fact that an electromagnet can be switched on and off was widely known.
notes.36: Prevention of overheating in a current-carrying wire was understood by the majority of candidates, but nearly half did not gain a mark here, often believing that thicker insulation would keep the wire cooler. �PAGE�6
